newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. says welcomes planned India-Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says welcomes planned India-Pakistan talks.

text.p: The United States on Friday welcomed the planned resumption of peace talks between rivals India and Pakistan, and urged both not to obstruct a treaty that would ban the production of nuclear bomb-making material.
"We are as pleased as any nation on earth that discussions between the two governments will begin shortly," U.S. ambassador to India Frank Wisner told a business conference.

Pakistan on Thursday said top foreign ministry officials of the two nations, which have fought three wars since independence in 1947, would meet in New Delhi on March 28. Bilateral talks stalled in 1994 over the disputed state of Jammu and Kashmir.
Wisner said he hoped the two neighbours would join the United States in supporting efforts to curb the spread of nuclear weapons.
India and Pakistan say they have no nuclear arms programmes but analysts say both nations could swiftly assemble a bomb.
"We appreciate the security needs of India and Pakistan," the ambassador said. "(But) I believe we share common goals."
"Most immediately, I hope the governments of these two countries will not stand in the way of a fissile material cutoff agreement."

Talks in Geneva on the proposed agreement have been deadlocked for several weeks since non-aligned countries, led by India and Pakistan, demanded that the five nuclear powers set a calendar for total nuclear disarmament.

"We appreciate India judges that it cannot today adhere to the (nuclear) Non-Proliferation Treaty or the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT). But we hope that in the future, circumstances will permit India to reassess its positions," Wisner said.

New Delhi last year blocked the passage of the CTBT, a proposed global treaty to ban test blasts, saying it was discriminatory and did not commit the nuclear powers to disarmament. Islamabad says it will not sign the pact unless India does so first.
Neither India nor Pakistan has signed the 1970 NPT, which bans nuclear testing. India, which held a nuclear test in 1974, says it does not plan further tests.
Wisner said expanding economic engagement was a key element of U.S. policy towards India, one of the world's 10 biggest emerging markets.
"We look to India to maintain and expand its commitment to liberalising its domestic economic policies and to removing barriers on trade that will maintain rapid growth," he said.
"We hope the time is not too distant when India will open her insurance markets and adopt full-scope patent protection."
